subject: Opposition to Extended Downtown (N. S. & W. Temple) Street Closures
comment: I strongly oppose this proposal. Closing major downtown corridors for up to eight months is excessive and unreasonable. North Temple, West Temple, and South Temple are essential arteries for residents, small businesses, transit riders, and daily commuters. An extended closure of this scale shifts the burden of a private event onto the broader public. Public safety can and should be addressed through targeted traffic control, limited-duration closures, and active management during peak times. An eight-month shutdown of key streets is not a balanced solution. Downtown businesses are still recovering and rely on predictable access. Residents deserve mobility and transparency. The City should not grant exclusive use of public right-of-way for such an extended period. This proposal goes too far and should not move forward in its current form.

subject: Street Noise
comment: City Council Members: I live in a 360+ unit apartment complex, and we can all hear the street noise on Main Street, West Temple, and Broadway (300 South) - especially on weekends. I have friends who live nearer State Street, where the street noise is even louder. Buskers who perform way past midnight are one problem, but the biggest problem is from loud motorcycles and souped-up cars. There is a noise ordinance, right? Shouldn't the Police enforce this ordinance for the health and safety of downtown residents, pedestrians, and other drivers? I understand that the police resources are stretched thin and that they often have more serious problems to deal with on weekends, but I wonder if there isn't more that they and you can do to alleviate the noise and safety concerns for the downtown residents and pedestrians. I believe that State Street is a State Highway, and the City may not have the option to place speed bumps on it. But if you can, that would certainly help to calm the traffic speed and noise. There are also other ways to mitigate the noise disruption to downtown residents. Do the Police have Decibel Meters? Shouldn't they be used to ticket the most egregious violators? If there are not enough officers to measure the noise levels and then chase down the noisemakers, could a Decibel Meter somehow be connected to an illuminated sign - much like those connected to a radar speed meter which flashes the speed limit and the speed of the violator? Placing such displays on State Street, Main Street, West Temple, 100 South, and/or Broadway would at least discourage the noisiest of the cars and motorcycles. Furthermore, can a 'Robocop' device be used to identify and ticket noisy offenders? There is a Police Substation on Regent Street just off 100 South between Main and State. There are always a lot of Police cars parked nearby. Could some of those vehicles be parked on State Street or Main Street - perhaps with their red and blue lights on - not necessarily flashing, but just ON - to let the drivers know that Police are watching? This might discourage some of the noisiest drivers. Any efforts you can make to mitigate the noise and improve the safety of downtown traffic would be appreciated. Thank you. Dave Jolley

subject: Constituent in support of HB381 S3 and related comments opposing SB242's anti-safe streets in SLC section Constituent in support of HB581 S3 and related comments opposing SB242's anti-safe streets in SLC section
comment: Dear Senator Plumb and fellow elected officials, As an e-bicycle must love our Electric Mobility Device Amendments, I am a constituent who owns two electric bicycles, a Riese and Muller cargo bike for bigger shopping errands and a Tern folding bike to get around town. These are in addition to my 4 other regular bicycles and my husband's collection of 6 more. We have always been a bike-ctl family thanks to living in historic East Central in Salt Lake City with good options besides driving thanks to being close to work, shopping, and UTA routes. That means we can afford to own a lot of bikes - nice ones. Bicycle and Electric Assist Bicycle Benefits A study in Scientific American revealed that cycling is the most energy-efficient mode of travel. "Humans aren't very efficient movers—until you put us on a bicycle, when we become some of the most energy-efficient land travelers in the animal kingdom." https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/e-human-on-a-bicycle-is-simple-the-most-efficient-forms-of-travel-in-the/ Plus, it's especially healthier, more fun, and pro-social. Except for the frequent fear factor on our many dangerous Utah and capital city streets. What is great about my electric bicycles? They extend my effective range, make starting up again at intersections more efficient, and reduce barriers like hills and wind. Plus did I mention fun? My cargo bike also gets a lot of positive comments out and around town - as a conservatively dressed woman of a certain age who is otherwise largely invisible I enjoy that. If you don't have an electric assist bicycle yet, I highly recommend test riding and online pre- I still ride my other bikes, but the e-bikes tend to get out more often these days. I assets at age 61 that's OK Better E-motorcycle regulation needed like in HB381 That said, I have been concerned about the proliferation of dangerous visiting throttle-only (non-pedal) pseudo-bicycles- little e-motorcycles. HB381 appropriately recognizes electric-assist pedal bicycles and throttle-only electric motorcycles as two very different categories and works to better address this. The forms and models of e-motorcycles have been changing rapidly and the laws have not kept up. It's not the fuel source; it's the propulsion and speed capabilities that make the biggest difference. Many of the reported injuries nationally are due to teens playing around on these more dangerous e-motors. Opposition to Helmet Laws for bicycles and electric bicycles (OK for e-motorcycles) I was concerned when it seemed that an under-21 helmet requirement could apply to all e-bikes for riders under 21; the bill summary isn't very clear. But in reading through HB381 S3 it looks like that is now revised 3" certain devices" so I am comfortable with that language. Studies show that helmet requirements for bicyclists can reduce head injuries to a limited extent but data shows that this may well be due to overall drop in cycling, not safer conditions for riders. This is not a good tradeoff when other things can reduce it "effectively If I never leave my house I will never be at risk of a crash or injury outdoors. That's not safety; that's being trapped. Helmet requirements may also stop some riders with fines even if they were riding safely, and this is often quite arbitrary. Minority and other disadvantaged riders may be more likely to be noticed by officers and subject to disproportionate enforcement; this is common with "jaywalking" (another very problematic category of violations). While I do support helmets as a smart choice for higher speed recreational riding and younger riders, in my opinion they should not be required by law. Yes, head injuries are a real risk from bad crashes. So are many other kinds of injuries bicyclists can't prevent. I also own several helmets but if I am just running errands on our better-designed streets like 200 and 300 South, I generally don't bother. At some point the responsibility must fall on riders, and on children's parents, to reduce personal choice unless appropriately. The need for Safe Streets By Design for Public Safety, Health, Economic Vitality, and Protection of Life To reduce systemic risks and also increase individual freedom of mobility, it is the responsibility of state and local governments to build and maintain safe, multimodal streets for all users. That is what generates the biggest safety benefit for all – including drivers – as shown by city after city, country after country, that actually do this. Far too many US and Utah civil engineers remain mired in out-of-date, dangerous street design models they were taught decades ago that have failed in both safety and efficient mobility in dense, complex city environments. Luckily, national guidelines such as NACTO https://nacto.org/ and even AASHTO are catching up. But local practices are too slow to change. The best cities in the world create safe urban environments by designing better and more complete street infrastructure or for pedestrians, cyclists, and riders alike. Most day-to day commuters and cyclists in these cities don't wear helmets, though many children do. I am getting old and impatient for safer streets for all. I fear I will never live to see the day Salt Lake City and other Utah cities level up to match the best cities in the country and world. Frankly, we are considering moving after retirement for this reason - we want to be able to age in place in a livable, active mobility, healthy community with clean air and safe streets. As someone who has donated so much personal time to community and volunteerism to improve our neighborhoods, city, and state, this is profoundly sad. Opposition to SB242's anti-safety anti-SLC dangerous language Especially now. The Legislature may make that even more impossible here in the capital city unless SB242 is amended. My recent visit to the Netherlands showed why safe streets by design works - they have focused for decades on safety by design: lower traffic speeds, separated and consistently designed street facilities including safe cycle networks, smart signaling, better transit. It was wonderful for all modes of travel - including having some of the most satisfied drivers in the world! Car traffic flows best when all the other modes are efficient and designed to have their own lanes - bicycle, sidewalk, transit, cars. Or compare the success of Oslo, Norway in Vision Zero and City livability but as compared to current conditions in Salt Lake City: https://thecityfix.com/blog/how-oslo-achieved-zero-pedestrian-and-bicycle-fatalities-and-how-others-can-apply-what-worked/ It's too many drivers and high speed, car-dependent, car-sewer car-filled streets and dangerous intersections that are creating the car traffic congestion and hazards. When people like me must bicycle in the car traffic lane because there is no bike lane, it is scary and also slows car traffic - not when I am in a bike lane! I experience this a lot on nearby streets 100 South, the west side of South Temple, 300 East, and more. As a driver, I am so frustrated when there are no bike lanes for the same reason. This is why a complete, connected network is so necessary. Car drivers get that - so should cyclists especially on our excessively wide streets. When I was a child, the majority of kids walked or bicycled to school. Now, that rate has plummeted and most kids get driven to school, trapping parents in the chase and impairing the health and well-being of children as well as creating a vicious cycle where the remaining kids who still try to walk or ride are threatened by all the car drivers. In the Netherlands, by contrast, most kids still ride or walk to school. Helmets don't keep them safe, good street design does. Unfortunately, Salt Lake City's roads remain super dangerous, especially wider streets with multiple lanes of car traffic and no bicycle lanes at all. Most Utah cities lack a proper network of protected bicycle infrastructure. My willingness and freedom to cycle gets more limited as I get older, sadly. The most effective way to reduce the risk of injury and death to bicycle riders - electric or regular - is to build safe, connected, protected networks of cycle lanes and intersections. Utah's generally big, wide streets give plenty of room to do just that. That is also why I objected so strongly to SB195's assault on SLC's already inadequate safe streets improvements last year. It proved to be a waste of taxpayer money as an unfunded mandate even as the study show that indeed, Salt Lake City's safe multimodal streets upgrades were not "impeded" car traffic. Done right, getting the people willing to take transit or bicycles plus the other proven Traffic Demand Management TDM strategies reduces congestion and traffic. In a growing urban area, it is the only way. SB242's section targeting SLC is much worse despite the results of SB195 that showed SLC is on the right track with rebuilding and redesigning its streets. As the Olympics approach again, SLC needs to keep improving, not fall behind other host cities. This language in SB242 needs to be removed. The Senate vote yesterday was a blow to public safety. May the House members be truly pro-life and stop this. In conclusion, please support HB581 S3 and oppose SB242 unless it is amended as described. Sincerely, Jen Colby, MPA Salt Lake City

subject: additional comments on rmf-45 to mu-5 zoning change
comment: Hey SLC Council and particularly my councilperson, Eva Lopez Chavez, As someone who lives across from the proposed rezoning at 539 S and 400 E I have already emailed comments to Olivia Cvetko during the 45 day comment period. I've received another piece of mail indicating there will be a public hearing. After reviewing the information from the developer's narrative https://www.slc.gov/planning/2025/10/17/openhouse2025-00704/ I can provide some direct feedback to that document as well. Developer: By building in these vibrant, accessible locations, we support walkability, encourage public transit use, and contribute to the long-term growth and vitality of the neighborhood. This project is unique for several reasons: -> This developer may talk about supporting walkability but when building The Citizen, the sidewalk they occupied remained unusable for nearly 2 years. While an inconvenience for me when I needed to go to the grocery store, this was a genuine hardship for neighbors who must use assisted mobility devices. Also, how do they encourage public transit use? Do they cover the UTA fares of their residents? If the argument is proximity then that is not much of an argument – i.e., the houses they intend to demolish are already in the same proximity and would also promote public transit use. Developer: First, as the second phase of an existing project next door, this development will feature studio, one- and two-bedroom units to help meet the high demand for cost-effective and attainable housing. The Citizen's units are already nearly fully occupied, demonstrating the strong market need. This project increases housing density in a walkable neighborhood while replacing three aging, dilapidated homes already surrounded by multifamily uses. -> A quick check on Zillow indicates 28 units are currently available at The Citizen. There likely will be many more available in the summer when the college students leave. Nearby rental communities are also struggling to fill their buildings. This property is simply adding to the glut of over-priced rental housing. Developer: Second, we plan to build ground floor commercial on just over 50% of the frontage facing 400 East. Although plans haven't been started, this is estimated to be at least 1,100 square feet. This commercial will serve as a community gathering place for a future commercial use. -> What does this last sentence even mean? If the developer can't be bothered to actually form a coherent vision of why they want to lower my property value by eliminating my view of the mountains then why should they be allowed to change the zoning laws simply for their convenience? Developer: In summary, Citizen 2 delivers meaningful community benefits that extend beyond the building itself, adding much-needed cost-effective housing, providing new neighborhood commercial in an area that doesn't have much of this type of commercial. These features directly support the City's goals for walkable, transit-oriented, and sustainable development. -> Cost-effective housing? By developer's own admission (found later in their proposal) it would be demolishing a currently occupied 2BR being rented at $1250 per month and a currently unoccupied 2BR which previously rented at $2300 per month. Compare that with a 2BR at The Citizen which starts at $2549 per month. It would be more appropriate if instead of using 'cost-effective' they used the phrase 'more expensive.' Groceries and electric are constantly getting more expensive. I don't see how a clear increase in rent is the right decision for this moment. -> As for adding to the amount of commercial space. I have a Smith's one block away, and within a half a mile there is Trolley Square, 900S, State St., Broadway, and everything downtown. I don't need more commercial near me and I don't want the associated parking headaches if they do manage to fill the commercial space. To close, If the developer wishes to buy the land and work within the existing medium-high residential rules then fine. But I urge the council to vote no on adjusting the rules to high-density mixed use. Thanks - Ben Baker

subject: SB242
comment: Hello, I'm writing to express my opposition to SB 242 - Transportation Amendments, particularly the addition of Section 72-20-101, Local Highway Mobility Plans, which targets traffic safety infrastructure in Salt Lake City. I live in Salt Lake City in the East Central neighborhood. I appreciate the city's recent complete, safer streets improvements and would like more of them. So I would like to see a substitute bill removing Section 72-20-101. I live with my daughter just below the University of Utah near 200 South. My daughter does not drive but is able to get to work using her bike and the readily available Trax and Bus system. The 200 South bus lanes are the most significant transit project since TRAX, facilitating more than 30 UTA buses per hour, plus the High Valley Transit 107 to Park City and, in the coming months and years, higher frequencies on the 2 bus and the launch of the Davis-SLC bus rapid transit service. If 200 South is "mitigated," removing or reducing the bus priority lanes, UTA and SLC cannot install transit priority signals and these critical transit services will be jeopardized. Bill supporters have been pointing to the fact that not everyone who travels downtown lives here. However, they are assuming that everyone who visits downtown drove there, and that there is no benefit gained from Salt Lake City residents who did not drive. Not only do visitors use transit—the Green Line airport Trax, the regional Frontrunner, which connects to local transit like the 200 South bus lanes—local car-free trips means less competition for street space, so less congestion and more parking availability. I love taking the Green Line to and from the airport from my home. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Monica Hilding

subject: Access restrictions on City-supported K7ARD
comment: Salt Lake City funds, houses, and integrates the K7ARD repeater system into its emergency and public-service communications. The City designates the Salt Lake Crossroads Amateur Radio Club as its operating partner. Materials describe Crossroads as providing auxiliary communications for the Department of Public Safety, including connecting fire stations, neighborhoods, and staff at planned City events. Access to K7ARD and good standing in Crossroads are required to participate in these City-supported operations. Crossroads began restricting my access after I challenged disability-rights violations and objected to mental-capacity framing. Crossroads has now banned me from the club and the system without review, appeal, or documented, neutrally applied standards. I provided Public Safety documentation of disability-linked access restrictions, including written references to mental health, temperament, and undefined behavioral standards. Public Safety responded that the City lacks authority over its publicly supported partner. The Mayor's Office of Access and Belonging followed suit, declining review under the City's ADA grievance procedure. Access to City-supported operations and infrastructure now rests on contradictory authority claims. Crossroads cited bylaw provisions that do not govern expulsion and claimed unilateral presidential control over membership and access. The City relies on this system for emergency operations, yet disclaims authority over access decisions. What action will the City take to prevent disability-based exclusion from K7ARD? Sabra Ewing City Council District 4

subject: Support for Recurring Nuisance Ordinance - City Corner Property
comment: Dear Council Members, I am writing in strong support of the proposed Recurring Nuisance Ordinance scheduled for vote on March 24. I live directly across the street from City Corner convenience store, and for an extended period of time, our neighborhood has experienced ongoing issues connected to this property. These concerns include repeated law enforcement activity, documented undercover investigations related to underage sales of alcohol and vaping products, and consistent traffic of minors entering and exiting the store. This is not an isolated incident. It has become a recurring disruption that affects the safety, stability, and quality of life of surrounding residents. Families live here. Children walk these streets daily. The continued pattern of activity at this location has created an environment that feels unsafe and attracts behavior that does not belong in a residential neighborhood. My understanding is that current enforcement tools often require lengthy criminal proceedings before meaningful action can be taken. In situations like this, that delay allows the nuisance activity to continue for years, despite clear and repeated concerns from neighbors and law enforcement. The Recurring Nuisance Ordinance would provide the City with a more timely and effective tool to address properties that repeatedly generate illegal or disruptive behavior. It creates accountability without requiring years of litigation while the surrounding community continues to bear the impact. This is not about targeting a specific business unfairly. It is about giving the City practical tools to protect neighborhoods when there is an established pattern of documented violations. I respectfully urge you to vote in favor of this ordinance so our community can have a safer and more stable environment. Thank you for your time and service to our city. Sincerely, Liz Rainey

subject: Good news that SB24232 failed in committee, please vote against unless Section 72-20-101 Local Highway Mobility Plans is removed Good news that SB242&2 failed in committee, please vote against unless Section 72-20-101 Local Highway Mobility Plans is removed
comment: Dear Members of the Transportation Committee, I was unable to attend the meeting yesterday but had sent comments in opposition to SB242 S2 and was grateful to learn that it failed to pass. Unfortunately, it returns for another round of review this afternoon. I remain adamantly opposed to SB 242 - Transportation Amendments - as long as it contains Section 72-20-101, Local Highway Mobility Plans, which targets traffic safety infrastructure in Salt Lake City. This undermines public safety, local control, and true freedom of mobility choice. It also violates the House of Representatives' mission statement, as I explain below. Please amend this bill to remove this section. If not, please vote against SB242. I see nothing in this omnibus bill that is critical for this session. Slipping poison pills like this section into an omnibus bill is poor policy making. I have already sent extensive comments about exactly why 72-20-101 is deeply flawed and dangerous. I incorporate them again by reference here. I earned a master's degree in public administration with honors from the University of Utah with a focus on planning and sustainability. I have been an advocate for safe streets, livable and economically vibrant cities, and active mobility for decades so I have expertise in these areas. I also travel a lot and have experienced the great transportation transformations in some of the best cities in the world. If this bill passes with Section 72-20-101, Salt Lake City will have no hope of joining them. I ask you to pause and consider why you are serving as an elected official for the State of Utah and the mission of the House of Representatives. I do believe that you embrace the mission statement and commitment to improving our state. So I don't understand why this bill has been drafted with the section that will not move us forward, but opposite. It is hard to be an expert in everything as a citizen lawmaker. Advocates for this bill section are mistaken. From the House website: https://house.utleg.gov/about-the-house/ The Utah House of Representatives, drawing on the diverse backgrounds and expertise of its members, identifies and leads on critical issues and best ideas in public policy. We honor our pioneer legacy by taking the long view. At the end of our service, we will leave the institution stronger, the State more financially stable, our education systems more nimble, forward-thinking, and responsive to the needs of both students and employers; our healthcare more innovative and affordable; our infrastructure better suited to meet the opportunities of tomorrow; our natural resources—air, water, and incomparable public lands—all better off, protected and preserved to enhance the quality of life for all Utahns. We are proud to represent our constituents and proud to call Utah home. As I read the mission statement, this bill as written violates numerous goals enumerated in it; specifically, the section targeting public safety improvements in Salt Lake City. Here is what I see that is so flawed – I edit the mission statement below as a commentary to reflect what SB242 would do. SB242 lands falls far behind the times on critical issues and best ideas in public policy; it forces dangerous, repeatedly disproven ideas about transportation planning on the capital city and UDOT. Sustainable Safety by design and freedom of mobility due to safe, efficient, multimodal options is best practice. Car dependence by design is what SB242 would create instead. SB242 Dis-honors our pioneer legacy by taking the long-sighted and backwards view. Both Joseph Smith Jr. and Brigham Young were forward-thinking urban planners with clear visions for the Plat of Zion. Salt Lake City was far ahead of its time according to historians as an orderly city complete with public and religious buildings, homes and apartments with gardens and orchards, and major grid streets that were wide enough to accommodate the transition from wagons to cars and also importantly, streetcars and trolleys. The latter system of streetcars was considered visionary for its time. Separated transit corridors on streets were accepted as appropriate street use, in their own dedicated lanes until the trolley lines were torn out and replaced by buses and cars. See Building Zion The Latter-day Saint Legacy of Urban Planning by Craig D. Galli in the BYU Studies Journal for a good article about this. Many cities in Utah including Salt Lake City, Ogden, and West Valley are restoring separated transit lanes on major multiline streets, like TRAX and 200 South and 3500 S. SB242 will leave ....the State more financially stable weakened due to the high cost of car-dependent street design, from the cost of crashes to air pollution to health costs to lower economic activity, and more. It also adds unfunded extra and unnecessary costs to UDOT and Salt Lake City. SB242 will leave our healthcare ....affordable expensive because of the combined health costs of preventable injuries from crashes and air pollution-caused diseases like asthma and heart disease; more than 50% of harmful air pollution is tailpipe emissions. Driving cars kills and injures people directly and indirectly. Traffic noise is also associated with stress and illness. Cities aren't loud, cars are loud (it's the tire noise too, not just the engines, horns, etc.) This drives up the cost of health care and insurance for all of us. SB242 will leave.....our infrastructure better unsuited to meet the opportunities of tomorrow. Car dependence by design and car clogged streets are so 1950. The best and most vibrant, livable, desirable cities in the world are moving far beyond what Salt Lake City has been doing towards multimodal, complete streets and cities filled with people -- not just cars. One city bus can carry the equivalent of 2 blocks worth of parked cars, especially since most people still drive alone. With the Olympics coming in 2034, host cities throughout Utah need to be rapidly adding real transportation options, not being blocked by the Legislature. Utah once again looks decades behind the times unless SB242 is amended. SB242 will leave ...our natural resources—air, water, and incomparable public lands—all better far worse off, protected and preserved degraded by pollution to enhance ruin the quality of life for all Utahans. As previously described, car dependence is causing excessive pollution, contributing to the loss of snowpack, and harming the health of our natural areas. Meanwhile cities like Paris and London and Oslo have seen remarkable, swift declines in particulate air pollution by redesigning streets and providing good transportation options other than driving. This leads to natural reductions in car traffic, and increases in bicycling and transit use. https://www.vox.com/energy-and-environment/23663628/paris-cut-air-pollution This can be done anywhere. SB242 will make that impossible in Utah's capital city, which would be truly devastating. "We are proud to represent our constituents and proud to call Utah home." -Mission statement To be truly proud to call Utah home, please vote against SB242 unless it is amended to remove Section 72-20-101, Local Highway Mobility Plans. SB242 Section 72-20-101 clearly violates the mission statement of the House of Representatives and threatens the wellbeing of Utah and its capital city. Thank you for your time and consideration. Jen Colby, MPA Bryant neighborhood
